q: A soft, early-drinking red grape of the Dao is known across the Spanish border as Mencia. What do the Portuguese call it?
exp: Jaen ripens early and gives colour and juicy red fruit but little structure. It is almost always blended with Touriga Nacional and Alfrocheiro rather than bottled on its own.

q: Between the Dao and the ocean sits a region that takes its name from the heavy clay under its vines. Which?
exp: Barro is Portuguese for clay, and the cold clay-limestone here holds water, ripens the fruit late and gives wines of formidable acidity. The Atlantic is close enough to make rot the grower's constant worry.

q: Late to ripen in a damp maritime autumn, and fierce with acid and tannin when it finally does, one grape dominates the reds of the clay belt near Coimbra. Which?
exp: Baga hangs on the vine into a wet October and was long fermented with all its stems, which is how it earned its reputation for being undrinkable young. Destemming and gentler handling have turned it into one of Portugal's most ageworthy reds.

q: Roast suckling pig is the dish every restaurant around Mealhada is judged on, and the local wine trade grew a speciality to match it. Which style?
exp: Bairrada has made bottle-fermented espumante since the late nineteenth century, and a bright, high-acid sparkling wine cuts the fat of leitao better than anything still. Baga itself is often the base, pressed pale.

q: Vines in the south share their ground with a wooded savannah of evergreen oaks grazed by black pigs, a farmed landscape called the montado. Which tree is it built on?
exp: Quercus suber and its holm-oak cousin shade the pasture, the acorns feed the pigs and the bark is stripped for stoppers. Wine, pork and cork all come off the same hectare.

q: In a handful of Alentejo cellars the wine still ferments and rests in tall clay vessels sealed with olive oil, opened by tradition on Saint Martin's Day. What is the vessel called?
exp: The technique is Roman and survived around Vidigueira, and the rules now recognise it in its own right. Tinaja is the Spanish equivalent and qvevri the Georgian one, while a lagar is the shallow stone trough used for treading grapes.

q: A red-fleshed French crossing found its most convincing home on the Alentejo plains, where it gives colour, structure and dark fruit. Which variety?
exp: Almost every red grape has clear juice, but this one stains from the pulp as well as the skin, which made it valuable to blenders everywhere. In the Alentejo it long outgrew that role and is now bottled on its own by the region's best estates.

q: Drought-tolerant and reliably even in ripening, one white grape anchors Alentejo blends and is usually paired with Arinto to keep the wine fresh. Which?
exp: Antao Vaz brings weight and ripe tropical fruit but not much acid, so Arinto is blended in to carry it. Roupeiro, also called Siria, is the region's other traditional white and fades quickly in bottle.

q: A grower in Reguengos and a grower in the Douro turn out to be working the same variety under two names. Which pair?
exp: The grape is Tempranillo, called Tinta Roriz in the north and Aragonez in the south. Renaming grapes region by region is the single hardest part of learning Portugal.

q: Deep Atlantic sand west of Sintra kept phylloxera out, so the vines there are still growing on their own roots. Which appellation?
exp: The louse cannot travel through pure sand, which leaves these among the very few ungrafted vineyards left in Europe. Growers dig trenches down through the dune to the clay beneath before they plant.

q: Sprawling low across the sand behind screens of woven cane, the vines of Colares are being defended against what?
opts: Spring frost rolling off the hills
exp: The vineyards sit almost on the beach, and unbroken ocean wind would shred the shoots and burn the leaves with salt. Keeping the canopy low and screened is the only way the fruit survives to October.

q: Ferociously tannic and needing a decade before it is civil, the red of the Sintra sand vineyards comes from which variety?
exp: Ramisco on ungrafted sand yields almost nothing and makes a wine that is severe in youth and remarkable at twenty years. Malvasia de Colares is the white counterpart in the same appellation.

q: British officers billeted near Lisbon during the Peninsular War took home a crisp white they called Lisbon Hock. Which small DOC made it?
exp: Bucelas lies in the Trancao valley just north of the city and makes white wine only, built on Arinto. The English taste for it faded, and the appellation is now down to a handful of producers.

q: After fortification, the winemaker returns the muscat skins to the fortified wine and leaves them there for months. What does that achieve?
opts: A far more intense grape and orange-peel aroma
A gentle sparkle, because the skins restart fermentation
A pale colour, because the skins reabsorb pigment
A dry finish, because the added spirit ferments out the sugar
exp: Alcohol is a better solvent for aromatic compounds than must is, so the maceration pulls terpenes out of the skins that fermentation alone would leave behind. It is the signature step of Moscatel de Setubal.

q: Warm sandy soils on the peninsula south of Lisbon suit a black grape that locals label Periquita. What is its proper name?
exp: Castelao is the mainstay of Palmela and of southern Portugal generally, giving a firm raspberry-and-tobacco red that softens over a few years. Periquita is a local name that a nineteenth-century brand made famous, which is why it still clings to the grape.

q: Casks shipped as ballast to the Indies and back came home tasting better than when they left, and an island trade rebuilt itself around that discovery. Which wine?
exp: Heat and motion in the hold cooked and aerated the wine, and the returned casks, vinho da roda, fetched a premium. Once the effect was understood, producers reproduced it on land rather than pay for the voyage.
